title: Pre-Emption Lawsuit in Bangladesh: How Co-Sharers Forcibly Buy Back Sold Land
metaTitle: Pre-Emption Lawsuit in Bangladesh: Section 96 SAT Act
metaDescription: Has a co-sharer sold family land to a stranger? Learn how to file a Pre-emption lawsuit under Section 96 SAT Act and forcibly buy back your land.
keywords: how to buy back ancestral land bangladesh
heroIntro: Few family shocks are as infuriating as discovering that your brother, uncle, or joint co-sharer has secretly sold an undivided piece of your ancestral land to an outside stranger without giving you the opportunity to purchase it. The first time you learn about the transfer is when an aggressive third party arrives with surveyors, planning to build a boundary wall through your family holding. In Bangladesh, the law strictly disfavors outside interlopers disrupting joint land holdings. Under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (SAT Act), co-sharers possess an extraordinary statutory power called the Right of Pre-emption (Ogrokroy). By filing a pre-emption lawsuit in the Civil Court and depositing the purchase consideration plus statutory compensation, you can compel the court to cancel the stranger's deed and forcibly transfer the title directly into your name.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer: Can You Legally Force an Outside Buyer to Sell Back Land in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: Yes. Under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (amended in 2006), if a co-sharer tenant transfers a portion of agricultural land to a stranger without giving notice to other co-sharers, any co-sharer by inheritance possesses the absolute statutory right of Pre-emption (Ogrokroy). The co-sharer can file a Pre-emption Case in the Court of the Senior Assistant Judge or Joint District Judge within two (2) months of the service of transfer notice, or within two months of gaining knowledge of the sale. The applicant must deposit the registered deed consideration money plus 25% statutory compensation into the court treasury. Upon verifying co-sharer status, the civil court passes a decree directing the stranger to execute a re-conveyance deed, restoring the land to the family.

sections.title: What Is the Right of Pre-emption (Ogrokroy) in Bangladesh?
sections.content:
The right of pre-emption—historically known in Bengal as Haq Shufa under Islamic jurisprudence and codified as Ogrokroy in modern statutory law—is a legal right conferred upon existing landowners to acquire property in preference to an outside stranger. The legislative purpose behind pre-emption is grounded in sound social policy: preventing the fragmentation of agricultural holdings, protecting the privacy and security of family residential compounds, and excluding hostile third-party speculators from disrupting joint holdings.

When a joint owner sells land without offering it first to co-heirs, the transaction is not automatically void, but it remains permanently defeasible. That means the sale stands subject to the superior right of the non-consenting co-sharers to step into the buyer's shoes. By invoking statutory pre-emption, you do not need to prove that the seller committed fraud or that the land was undervalued; the mere fact that you are a legitimate co-sharer by inheritance and were bypassed gives you the statutory power to buy back the property through judicial mandate.

sections.title: Section 96 State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950
sections.content:
The primary governing statute for pre-emption of agricultural land in Bangladesh is Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (SAT Act). The section underwent a major legislative overhaul through the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act 2006, which introduced streamlined rules to curb frivolous litigation while reinforcing the primacy of family co-heirs.

Under Section 96(1), if a portion or share of a holding of land is transferred, one or more co-sharer tenants of the holding may apply to the court for the portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves. The statute mandates that the application must be instituted in the civil court of the lowest grade having territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction (typically the Senior Assistant Judge or Joint District Judge Court). Once the statutory conditions are met, the court has no discretion to refuse; granting pre-emption is a mandatory statutory duty.

sections.title: Who Is Eligible: Co-Sharers by Inheritance vs. Purchase
sections.content:
A pivotal reform introduced by the 2006 Amendment to Section 96 SAT Act was clarifying the hierarchy of eligible applicants. Prior to 2006, adjacent landowners (contiguous plot owners) could also file pre-emption suits, creating endless litigation among neighbors. Today, the law establishes strict eligibility:

  • Co-sharer by Inheritance (Primary Right): A person who inherited an undivided share of the land from a common ancestor. Co-sharers by inheritance enjoy the highest, indisputable priority. If a co-sharer by inheritance applies, their claim defeats all other classes of claimants.
  • Co-sharer by Purchase: A person who acquired an undivided share in the holding through a registered deed of purchase. Under the amended law, a co-sharer by purchase can only claim pre-emption if no co-sharer by inheritance applies.
  • Exclusion of Contiguous Neighbors: Under the amended Section 96, adjacent/neighboring plot owners who do not share title in the holding can no longer claim pre-emption over agricultural land, preventing predatory boundary lawsuits.

sections.title: Mandatory Court Deposit: Consideration Plus 25% Compensation
sections.content:
The single most critical procedural requirement of a Section 96 pre-emption case is the statutory deposit. Unlike general civil lawsuits where court fees are nominal, pre-emption requires the applicant to put their money on the table immediately upon filing.

Under Section 96(3) of the SAT Act, the application will not be entertained unless the applicant, at the time of making the application, deposits in the court:

  1. The Consideration Amount: The exact purchase price stated on the face of the registered sale deed executed in favor of the stranger.
  2. 25% Statutory Compensation: An additional statutory compensation equal to twenty-five percent (25%) of the stated consideration value, awarded to the purchaser for being deprived of the land.
  3. 8% Annual Interest: Simple interest calculated at eight percent (8%) per annum on the consideration amount from the date of deed execution to the date of filing the application.

If the applicant fails to deposit the full statutory sum via treasury challan concurrently with the application, the petition is summarily rejected as legally incompetent. No extension of time is granted for this deposit.

sections.title: Strict Statutory Limitation Deadlines: The Two-Month Rule
sections.content:
The law of limitation in pre-emption cases is unforgiving. Under Section 96(1) of the SAT Act, an application for pre-emption must be made within:

  • Two (2) Months: Within two months from the date of the service of official notice of transfer under Section 89 of the SAT Act. When a deed is registered at the Sub-Registry Office, the Sub-Registrar is legally required to issue a formal transfer notice to all recorded co-sharers.
  • Two Months from Knowledge (Max 3 Years): If the seller and buyer colluded to conceal the sale and no official notice was served, the co-sharer must file within two (2) months from the date they first acquired knowledge of the fraudulent sale. However, the application must in all events be filed within three (3) years from the date of registration of the deed.

Waiting even one day past the two-month deadline from the date of confirmed knowledge can prove fatal to your claim. Your advocate must plead the exact date and mode of gaining knowledge in the plaint with meticulous precision.

sections.title: Pre-Emption for Non-Agricultural Land: Section 24 NAT Act
sections.content:
While Section 96 SAT Act governs agricultural holdings, urban real estate (commercial shops, residential plots in cities and municipalities) is governed by Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 (NAT Act). While the underlying objective remains the same, several procedural distinctions apply:

Under Section 24 of the NAT Act, the statutory compensation deposited with the court is five percent (5%) of the purchase consideration, accompanied by interest at the rate of 6.25% per annum. Furthermore, under the NAT Act, contiguous landowners (neighbors whose land touches the boundary of the transferred plot) retain the legal standing to claim pre-emption if no co-sharer exercises their right. Understanding whether the land is classified in the government Khatian as agricultural (Nal, Doba) or non-agricultural (Bastu, Dukan, Commercial) dictates which statute must be invoked.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Civil Court Procedure and Reconveyance
sections.content:
The judicial progression of a pre-emption lawsuit follows a structured timeline:

  1. Filing and Challan Deposit: The advocate files a Miscellaneous Case under Section 96 SAT Act, annexing certified copies of the deed, Khatian, and the treasury challan proving deposit of the consideration plus 25% compensation.
  2. Service of Summons: The court issues notices to the purchaser (transferee) and the seller (transferor), requiring them to show cause within a specified date.
  3. Injunction Against Possession & Construction: Concurrently, the advocate moves an application under Order 39 CPC for a temporary injunction restraining the purchaser from constructing structures, digging foundations, or transferring the land to fourth parties.
  4. Evidence & Final Order: The court examines proof of co-sharership (CS, SA, RS, and City/BS Khatians) and verifies the limitation timeline. Upon satisfaction, the court allows the pre-emption case.
  5. Deed Execution by Court: The court directs the purchaser to execute and register a re-conveyance deed in favor of the applicant. If the purchaser refuses to sign, the judge executes and registers the deed under the official court seal, and the court bailiff delivers physical possession to the applicant.

sections.title: Comparison Table: Section 96 SAT Act vs. Section 24 NAT Act
sections.content:
The table below summarizes the vital legal distinctions between pre-emption of agricultural versus non-agricultural land in Bangladesh:

Legal FeatureSection 96 SAT Act 1950 (Agricultural)Section 24 NAT Act 1949 (Non-Agricultural)
Land ClassificationAgricultural land (Nal, Chala, Crop fields)Urban, homestead, commercial, shop plots
Statutory Compensation25% of registered purchase consideration5% of registered purchase consideration
Annual Interest Rate8% simple interest per annum6.25% simple interest per annum
Adjacent Neighbor RightsCompletely abolished by 2006 AmendmentPermitted if no co-sharer applies
Primary PriorityCo-sharer by inheritance has absolute priorityCo-sharer tenant holds primary priority

Accurately identifying the land classification ensures that your pre-emption deposit and petition are legally unassailable from day one.

sections.title: Illustrative Scenario: Recovering Ancestral Land in Cumilla
sections.content:
The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) illustrates how an aggrieved co-sharer used Section 96 to buy back stolen family land in Cumilla:

Three brothers jointly inherited an undivided 30-decimal agricultural parcel in Debidwar, Cumilla. Two brothers lived in Dhaka working in private firms, while the youngest brother remained in the village. In early 2024, the youngest brother, facing gambling debts, secretly sold his undivided 10-decimal share to an influential local brickfield owner for BDT 12,00,000, registering the deed at Debidwar Sub-Registry Office. The buyer deliberately omitted serving notice to the two elder brothers. Four months later, when the elder brothers visited the village for Eid, they found laborers digging soil across the plot.

The brothers engaged a civil litigation advocate. Within 48 hours, the advocate obtained a certified copy of the sale deed from the Sub-Registry Office. The deed stated a consideration of BDT 12,00,000. Working swiftly to meet the strict two-month limitation from the date of knowledge, the advocate filed a Miscellaneous Case under Section 96 of the SAT Act in the Court of the Senior Assistant Judge, Debidwar. Concurrently, the brothers deposited BDT 12,00,000 (consideration) plus BDT 3,00,000 (25% statutory compensation) plus statutory interest into the government treasury via court challan.

The advocate immediately secured an ad-interim injunction under Order 39 CPC restraining the brickfield owner from excavating soil. In court, the buyer argued that the brothers knew of the sale earlier, but could produce no proof of written notice under Section 89. The court held that the elder brothers were co-sharers by inheritance with superior statutory rights. The Senior Assistant Judge allowed the pre-emption case, directed the deposit to be paid to the buyer, and ordered the buyer to execute a deed of re-conveyance. When the buyer evaded, the judge executed the registered deed under the court's official seal, successfully returning the 10 decimals to the ancestral family.

faqs.question: What is a Pre-emption (Ogrokroy) lawsuit in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Pre-emption is a statutory lawsuit where a co-sharer of land exercises their legal right to forcibly buy back a portion of the property sold by another co-heir to an outside stranger, upon depositing the purchase price plus statutory compensation into court.

faqs.question: How much money must be deposited to file a pre-emption case under Section 96 SAT Act?
faqs.answer: You must deposit the exact consideration money written on the registered deed, plus 25% statutory compensation, plus 8% annual interest calculated from the date of deed registration to the date of filing.

faqs.question: What is the time limit to file a pre-emption case in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Under Section 96 of the SAT Act, you must file within two (2) months of receiving official notice of transfer, or within two months of learning of the sale, subject to an outside maximum cap of three (3) years from the date of deed registration.

faqs.question: Can an adjacent neighbor claim pre-emption on agricultural land?
faqs.answer: No. The State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act 2006 abolished pre-emption rights for contiguous/adjacent neighbors over agricultural land. Only co-sharers by inheritance and co-sharers by purchase can claim pre-emption under Section 96.

faqs.question: Can an outside buyer refuse to sell the land back if pre-emption is granted?
faqs.answer: No. Once the civil court passes a pre-emption decree, the buyer is legally obligated to execute a re-conveyance deed. If the buyer refuses or evades, the civil court judge executes and registers the deed under the court's official seal.

faqs.question: What happens if the seller wrote an artificially high price on the deed to block pre-emption?
faqs.answer: If the parties inflated the registered deed price to discourage pre-emption, the applicant must initially deposit the stated deed amount, but can challenge the valuation during trial. The court can order an inquiry to determine true market value and order a partial refund.

faqs.question: Can I stop the buyer from building structures while the pre-emption case is ongoing?
faqs.answer: Yes. Your advocate will file an application for a Temporary Injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 CPC. The court will issue an injunction restraining the buyer from constructing buildings, digging soil, or transferring the land until final judgment.

faqs.question: Can an overseas Bangladeshi (NRB) file a pre-emption lawsuit from abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes. An NRB co-heir can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, empowering a trusted relative or lawyer in Bangladesh to file the petition and deposit the treasury funds.
